reverse_outline.summary: Chapter promise: learn ten revenue models, their KPIs and system demands, then judge three Veldmark proposals
Business stake: mature portals grow by changing what is sold; unmeasurable models leak revenue and drive away supply
Architect stake: each model needs specific systems, and paid products tie monetization to search ranking
Key points: unit of charge is the architectural choice, monetization spends liquidity, pricing power is conditional
Three failure patterns addressed: Vanity Liquidity, Multiplier Creep, Billing by Guesswork
Classifieds usually charge for access to attention rather than the transaction, though some now charge for transactions
Defines a monetization model as who pays, which unit, which moment, which pricing basis, each mapping to a system
Places the chapter in Part VI and lays out its roadmap / names neighbouring chapters that own adjacent topics

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Veldmark: Where Does the Next Euro Come From? ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Veldmark's revenue-growth mandate and Olivier's three proposals: Tradeyard visibility, Motorvane per-lead, Hearthly commission share

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Veldmark: Where Does the Next Euro Come From? ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Ingrid reframes the pricing proposals as architecture decisions using four questions

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Concepts: What a Listing Marketplace Sells ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Two-sided price structure: the free side subsidised because it creates the value professionals pay for

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Concepts: What a Listing Marketplace Sells ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Charging the demand side works only under scarce supply, illustrated by ImmoScout24 Plus subscriptions

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Concepts: What a Listing Marketplace Sells ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Professionals buy a probability of a match, so every paid product spends organic liquidity

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Concepts: What a Listing Marketplace Sells ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: The unit of charge is the key fact of a model, revealed by the denominator of a portal's KPI

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Concepts: What a Listing Marketplace Sells ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Source citations for the KPI table

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Concepts: What a Listing Marketplace Sells ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: Defines the recurring KPIs ARPA, ARPR and take rate, with Autotrader's arithmetic check

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Concepts: What a Listing Marketplace Sells ¶7
reverse_outline.summary: Comparing KPI denominators reveals four business types; classifieds lack GMV so report ARPA-like measures

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Concepts: What a Listing Marketplace Sells ¶8
reverse_outline.summary: Defines value-added services as paid presentation or ranking options, as OLX's ranking model shows
Introduces the ten revenue models and how groups combine them, with a comparison table
Insertion fees charge sellers to publish, with Scout24 and Autotrader evidence of price sensitivity
Systems insertion fees need: listing-time pricing, pay-before-publish checkout, moderation refunds, billable expiry
Insertion fees spend supply but also act as a trust filter against fraud
Paid visibility's three mechanics: bumps, top or featured slots, and highlights
Systems paid visibility needs: scheduler, separate ranking timestamp, slot rotation, mandatory paid label, delivery measurement
Paid visibility spends relevance; OLX shows search changes are monetization changes
Professional subscriptions: tiered monthly contracts granting slots, boosts, tools and prominence
Rightmove and CarGurus evidence that subscriptions are commitments plus metered extras with auto-renewing terms
Autotrader's ARPR growth decomposed into three levers
Stock lever lets dealers cut spend by listing fewer cars, making slot design a revenue decision / bundling AI tools inside packages as a pricing argument
Systems subscriptions need: contract management, quota enforcement across feeds, invoicing, account hierarchy, ROI reporting
Subscriptions spend little liquidity but expose the portal to concentrated customers and package competition for prominence
Depth products in seller-pays property: revenue is listings times yield, shown by REA growth and Hemnet's volume loss
Systems depth products need: mid-life per-listing upgrades, agent-mediated billing, per-listing delivery evidence
Depth products spend supply; per-listing models are exposed to sellers leaving, defended by free entry
Three lead-fee variants documented by Zillow: cost per lead, share of voice, pay at close
European example: AVIV France's commission-share model for seller leads
Lead models need billable-lead definitions, allocation engines or outcome pipelines; revenue rests on attribution
Lead fees spend trust, incentivising manufactured contacts, disputes and off-platform diversion
Transactional fees and take rates, illustrated by eBay's take rate and Vinted's buyer fee
Classifieds adding transactions report small revenue shares and lower margins, per Adevinta
Transactional systems needs, plus buyer fees putting pricing on the search read path and buyer protection as a liability
Transactional fees spend margin and simplicity, with liquidity effects depending on category trust and payment norms
Advertising monetises audience; sponsored listings run in search; advertising most exposed to Vanity Liquidity
Data and SaaS sales to professionals bring separate billing and a neutrality governance problem
Financing and insurance referrals need partner APIs, consented handoff and commission reconciliation
Consumer subscriptions gate search advantages for paying buyers and raise a fairness question

reverse_outline.summary: Legend and provenance note for the capability matrix

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Architecture: The Systems Each Model Requires ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Catalog, pricing, entitlements, ranking hooks and metering form a shared core; boundaries matter most

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Architecture: The Systems Each Model Requires ¶4

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Architecture: The Systems Each Model Requires ¶5

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Architecture: The Systems Each Model Requires ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: Ranking consumes monetization inputs under ranking-team guardrails, preventing Multiplier Creep

reverse_outline.summary: Mature portals grow revenue per customer through annual price-and-product events while customer counts stay flat

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice: Pricing Power and Its Limits ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Price changes must ship as dated, reversible data releases rather than code changes

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice: Pricing Power and Its Limits ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Concentrated professional customers limit pricing power, as Autotrader's forecourt loss despite market leadership shows

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice: Pricing Power and Its Limits ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Commercial model changes need staged rollout tooling like risky code changes

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice: Pricing Power and Its Limits ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: OLX case: naive dashboards misjudged package value due to selection bias; causal matching revealed large uplift

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice: Pricing Power and Its Limits ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: ROI dashboards must use causal measurement backed by an experimentation platform, or renewals get renegotiated
Every model spends organic liquidity, so each needs a guardrail metric owned outside the revenue team
Guardrails measure supply, relevance, trust or experience, not revenue, defined in the governed metrics layer

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Veldmark Worked Example: Revenue Mix and Three Proposals ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Motorvane's per-slot value of about €15 a month shows its revenue is exposed to dealers cutting stock

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Veldmark Worked Example: Revenue Mix and Three Proposals ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Olivier's case for Tradeyard: Top listing underpriced and Spotlight adds a premium step

reverse_outline.summary: Forum's four-question analysis of Proposal 1: weak entitlement system, high liquidity cost, buyers notice first

reverse_outline.summary: Proposal 1 deferred pending ranking review and explicit paid fields; Top listing price rise alone approved

reverse_outline.summary: Olivier's case for Motorvane: bill qualified leads above a package allowance

reverse_outline.summary: Proposal 3 piloted in Lyon for 2028 with finance-agreed estimation, since revenue depends on partner reconciliation
Comparison table of all models: each fits only where its unit matches selling and delivery can be counted
Model complexity compounds on a shared page; Veldmark's June ranking policy capped paid positions and withdrew Spotlight
Verticals change payer, center of gravity, KPI, lead value and distinctive systems
Monetization model is least shareable; share the systems underneath, leave packages and prices to brands
Most failures come from launching models before counting, capping and proving systems exist
Vanity Liquidity: selling views loses renewals; report contacts with shared definitions in billing and dashboards
Multiplier Creep: uncapped paid positions gradually fill the first page until contact rates fall
Billing by Guesswork: products added as scattered code conditions leave entitlements unprovable
Recap of misleading ROI dashboards and price events shipped as code
Lead fees without definitions and dispute process get defined by disputes
Outcome-based revenue reported only by professionals is trust, not billing, and needs estimation before launch
Paid boosts can serve scammers; run them through risk checks and refund on moderation removal
Chief Architect's five decisions: separate choice from implementation, explicit paid effects, guardrails, readiness card, causal measurement
Long-term signals to watch: outcome-dependent revenue, paid-stock downgrades, paid first-page share, price-event engineering cost
Ten review questions for any revenue proposal, extending Ingrid's four
Conclusion: model choice is choosing the unit, system of record and liquidity spend, as the three Veldmark decisions showed
Hand-off: all models share a commercial core Veldmark lacks, designed in the next chapter on products and entitlements

results.finding: The spec says the Hemnet figures show that yield can grow while volume falls. The draft gives ARPL +12.4% and net sales −23.1% but never states that listing volume fell, then refers to 'the volume loss' as if it had been stated; both flow readers had to infer it. The statistic's point is left to the reader.
